steps.message: You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

Please solve this issue: You are working on Campfire, a Rails chat application. Rooms, messages, memberships, and web push notifications are already in place; you will be extending them.

Feel free to store any design notes/insights that could be useful for future steps in the docs/ folder.

Follow the codebase conventions.

Our QA auto-tests drive the app in a browser and rely on the labels in quotes in each task. Keep them exactly as written, as visible text, a <label>, a placeholder, or an aria-label.

The QA auto-tests also expect:

- Switches are checkboxes (a styled switch is fine if a real checkbox sits under it).
- Confirmations use the browser's native `confirm()` dialog.

Some bots misbehave: they flood rooms, or their webhooks keep failing.

> As an administrator, I want misbehaving bots to be stopped automatically,
> and I want to decide when they come back.

Flooding:

- A bot may post at most 10 messages in any 10 seconds. Messages posted through the API and webhook replies both count.
- The message that goes over the limit is rejected and starts a 30-second cooldown. During the cooldown, the posting endpoint responds with `429 Too Many Requests` and a `Retry-After` header (seconds left), and webhook replies are not posted.
- Five more attempts to post during the same cooldown suspend the bot.

Failing webhooks:

- A failed delivery is any response other than `2xx`, a timeout, or a connection error.
- Ten failed deliveries in a row suspend the bot. A successful delivery resets the count.

A suspended bot:

- gets `403 Forbidden` from the posting endpoint;
- receives no webhooks;
- keeps its rooms and messages, and still counts towards its owner's bot limit;
- stays listed on the bots page and shows as "Suspended", with the reason.

Only administrators can reactivate a suspended bot, from the bots page: a "Reactivate" button that asks for confirmation. The limits above are fixed in code; they have no settings.

- `VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY`/`VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY` - a key pair used for sending Web Push notifications.

You can generate them by running:

```sh
docker run --rm ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire:latest script/admin/generate-secrets
```

It prints a fresh set of values ready to set as environment variables:

```
SECRET_KEY_BASE=...
VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY=...
VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY=...
```

Keep them safe and reuse the same values across restarts and upgrades - changing them later will invalidate sessions and push notification subscriptions.

#### SSL

If you want the Campfire container to handle its own SSL (HTTPS) automatically (via Let's Encrypt), you just need to specify the domain name that you're running it on.
You can do that with the `TLS_DOMAIN` environment variable.

> [!NOTE]
> If you're using SSL, you'll want to allow traffic on ports 80 and 443.

So if you were running on `chat.example.com` you could enable SSL like this:

```sh
docker run --publish 80:80 --publish 443:443 --env TLS_DOMAIN=chat.example.com ...
```

If you are terminating SSL in some other proxy in front of Campfire, or aren't using SSL at all (for example, if you want to run it locally on your laptop), then you should set `DISABLE_SSL=true` instead and just publish port 80:

```sh
docker run --publish 80:80 --env DISABLE_SSL=true ...
```

#### Error reporting (optional)

To enable error reporting to Sentry in production, supply your DSN in the `SENTRY_DSN` environment variable.
To disable Sentry initialization entirely, set `SKIP_TELEMETRY=true`.

### Example

Putting it all together, here's a complete `docker run` invocation:

```sh
docker run \
  --name campfire \
  --publish 80:80 --publish 443:443 \
  --restart unless-stopped \
  --volume campfire:/rails/storage \
  --env SECRET_KEY_BASE=$YOUR_SECRET_KEY_BASE \
  --env VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY=$YOUR_PUBLIC_KEY \
  --env VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY=$YOUR_PRIVATE_KEY \
  --env TLS_DOMAIN=chat.example.com \
  ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire:latest
```

And here's an equivalent `docker-compose.yml` that you could use to run Campfire via `docker compose up`:

```yaml
services:
  web:
    image: ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire:latest
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "80:80"
      - "443:443"
    environment:
      - SECRET_KEY_BASE=abcdefabcdef
      - TLS_DOMAIN=chat.example.com
      - VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY=myvapidprivatekey
      - VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY=myvapidpublickey
    volumes:
      - campfire:/rails/storage

volumes:
  campfire:
```

### First run

When you start Campfire for the first time, you'll be guided through creating an admin account.

> [!TIP]
> The email address of this admin account will be shown on the login page so that people who forget their password know who to contact for help.
> (You can change this email later in the settings.)

Campfire is single-tenant: any rooms designated "public" will be accessible by all users in the system.
To support entirely distinct groups of customers, you would deploy multiple instances of the application.

### Upgrading

All of Campfire's state lives in the mounted volume, so upgrading is a matter of pulling a newer image and recreating the container:

```sh
docker pull ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire:latest
```

Any pending database migrations run automatically when the container boots.

### Backups

To back up your instance, back up the contents of the `/rails/storage` volume.

Because the SQLite database may be written to at any moment, you shouldn't copy its files directly while Campfire is running.
Instead, first run `script/admin/prepare-backup` inside the running container to produce a consistent snapshot of the database (it's written to `storage/backups/` inside the volume):

```sh
docker exec campfire script/admin/prepare-backup
```

(If you're using Docker Compose, replace `docker exec campfire` with `docker compose exec web`)

Then archive the whole storage volume to a file on the host:

```sh
docker run --rm \
  --user root \
  --volume campfire:/rails/storage \
  --volume "$PWD":/backup \
  ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire:latest \
  tar czf "/backup/campfire-backup.tar.gz" -C /rails storage
```

This gives you a `campfire-backup.tar.gz` in your current directory containing the database snapshot and all uploaded files.
Copy it somewhere safe, ideally off the machine.

To restore, extract the archive back into a (stopped) instance's volume, and replace the live database with the snapshot:

```sh
docker run --rm \
  --user root \
  --volume campfire:/rails/storage \
  --volume "$PWD":/backup \
  ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire:latest \
  bash -c "tar xzf /backup/campfire-backup.tar.gz -C /rails &&
           cp /rails/storage/backups/production.sqlite3 /rails/storage/db/production.sqlite3 &&
           rm -f /rails/storage/db/production.sqlite3-wal /rails/storage/db/production.sqlite3-shm &&
           chown -R rails:rails /rails/storage"
```

Then start Campfire again.

module Message::Mentionee
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  INLINE_WRAPPER_TAGS = %w[ a b code del em i ins mark s small span strong sub sup u ].freeze

  def mentionees
    room.users.where(id: mentioned_users.map(&:id))
  end

  def plain_text_without_mention(user)
    return "" unless body.body

    stripped_fragment = body.body.fragment.update do |source|
      source.css(ActionText::Attachment.tag_name).each do |node|
        remove_mention_node(node) if ActionText::Attachment.from_node(node).attachable == user
      end
    end

    ActionText::Content.new(stripped_fragment, canonicalize: false).to_plain_text.gsub(/\u00A0/, " ").strip
  end

  private
    def mentioned_users
      if body.body
        body.body.attachables.grep(User).uniq
      else
        []
      end
    end

    def remove_mention_node(node)
      target = node
      while target.parent && INLINE_WRAPPER_TAGS.include?(target.parent.name) &&
            target.parent.children.all? { |child| child == target || (child.text? && child.content.empty?) }
        target = target.parent
      end

      if target.previous&.text? && target.next&.text? &&

      elsif target.next.nil? && target.previous&.text?
        target.previous.content = target.previous.content.sub(/[ \t\u00A0]+\z/, "")
      end

      target.remove
    end

#!/usr/bin/env ruby

require "json"
require "yaml"

class ProcessMonitor
  SIGNALS = %w[ INT TERM CLD ]

  def initialize(procfile)
    @procs = process_list(procfile)
    handle_signals

    @procs.each &:start
    @procs.each &:wait
  end

  private
    def process_list(procfile)
      config = YAML.load_file(procfile)
      config.map { |name, cmd| MonitoredProcess.new(name, cmd) }
    end

    def handle_signals
      SIGNALS.each do |signal|
        Signal.trap(signal) do
          @procs.each &:terminate
        end
      end
    end
end

class MonitoredProcess
  def initialize(name, cmd)
    @name, @cmd = name, cmd
  end

  def start
    @pid = Process.spawn(@cmd)
  end

  def wait
    Process.wait @pid
  rescue Errno::ECHILD
    nil
  end

  def terminate
    Process.kill "TERM", @pid
  rescue Errno::ESRCH
    nil
  end
end

**A Eureka Moment: SQLite for Critical State Management**

Okay, this is huge. I've been digging into the application architecture across environments, and a significant pattern has emerged. Across `test`, `development`, and `production`, we're leveraging SQLite in a way I hadn't fully appreciated, and the implications are significant.

In `test`, we're using a `null_store` for caching, and Redis isn't even running, which is expected. Development is similar, with the `null_store` unless a specific file exists. This isn't that surprising. But, the key takeaway is production, where `web` and `workers` are separate OS processes, but *both* share the same SQLite database. This shared SQLite database with `default_transaction_mode: immediate` is the linchpin.

The real breakthrough here is that this SQLite setup allows us to reliably persist crucial state – rate limiting, cooldowns, webhook failure counts, and suspension data – *everywhere*. It works in `test` *without* Redis. It works in `development` *without* Redis caching enabled. And, critically, it works in *production* across multiple Puma threads AND separate Resque worker processes, all within atomic, `IMMEDIATE` transactions thanks to `with_lock` and standard `transaction` blocks. We have ACID transactions across processes in SQLite! Even better, it plays nicely with Rails' time manipulation methods (`travel`, `travel_to`, `freeze_time`), as `Time.current` is respected!

Wait, let's back up and make sure I'm following. If we're storing these critical states in SQLite, then:

*   Does it work in the Puma and Resque architecture? YES! Shared SQLite is the magic.
*   Does it work with `IMMEDIATE` transactions in SQLite? YES! Concurrency is serialized without race conditions.
*   Does it work when the Rails cache is the `:null_store`? YES! Cache is irrelevant here.
*   Does it work without Redis running? YES! This is huge for test suite speed.

However, the use of `authenticate_bot` needs to be carefully modified to prevent returning `401 Unauthorized` for a suspended bot's key and instead provide a `403`. class Room < ApplicationRecord
  has_many :memberships, dependent: :delete_all do
    def grant_to(users)
      room = proxy_association.owner
      Membership.grant_for(Array(users).collect { |user| { room_id: room.id, user_id: user.id, involvement: room.default_involvement } })
    end

    def revoke_from(users)
      destroy_by user: users
    end

    def revise(granted: [], revoked: [])
      transaction do
        grant_to(granted) if granted.present?
        revoke_from(revoked) if revoked.present?
      end
    end
  end

  has_many :users, through: :memberships
  has_many :messages, dependent: :destroy

  belongs_to :creator, class_name: "User", default: -> { Current.user }

  validate :direct_rooms_keep_their_type, on: :update

  scope :opens,           -> { where(type: "Rooms::Open") }
  scope :closeds,         -> { where(type: "Rooms::Closed") }
  scope :directs,         -> { where(type: "Rooms::Direct") }
  scope :without_directs, -> { where.not(type: "Rooms::Direct") }

  scope :ordered, -> { order("LOWER(name)") }

  class << self
    def create_for(attributes, users:)
      transaction do
        create!(attributes).tap do |room|
          room.memberships.grant_to users
        end
      end
    end

    def original
      order(:created_at).first
    end
  end

  def receive(message)
    unread_memberships(message)
    push_later(message)
    deliver_webhooks_later(message)
  end

  def open?
    is_a?(Rooms::Open)
  end

  def closed?
    is_a?(Rooms::Closed)
  end

  def direct?
    is_a?(Rooms::Direct)
  end

  def default_involvement
    "mentions"
  end

  private
    # Open and closed rooms convert into each other freely. A direct room can't become
    # either: its participants agreed to a private conversation, not to one whose
    # audience someone else gets to widen afterwards.
    def direct_rooms_keep_their_type
      if type_changed? && type_was == "Rooms::Direct"
        errors.add :type, "can't be changed for a direct room"
      end
    end

    def unread_memberships(message)
      memberships.visible.disconnected.where.not(user: message.creator).update_all(unread_at: message.created_at, updated_at: Time.current)
    end

    def push_later(message)
      Room::PushMessageJob.perform_later(self, message)
    end

    def deliver_webhooks_later(message)
      return if message.creator.bot?

      Webhook.where(user: message.mentionees.active.bot).find_each do |webhook|
        webhook.deliver_later(message)
      end
    end

**Detailed Analysis of Bot Suspension and Flooding Mechanics**

Okay, let's break this down systematically. I need to make sure I'm solid on how bot suspension, flooding, and cooldowns work, and how they should be implemented. I'm focusing on making everything as clean and understandable as possible, avoiding kludges and fragile workarounds.

First, the core concept: bot suspension is *not* a status within the account lifecycle (like "active" or "banned"). It's a temporary state reflecting a *violation* – either flooding or excessive webhook failures. This means keeping the `status` enum clean: just `active`, `deactivated`, and `banned`, *not* "suspended."  Instead, I'll use `suspended_at` and `suspension_reason` columns (or perhaps a dedicated `bot_suspensions` table) to track the suspension state.  This way, `User.active` queries *always* mean "not deactivated and not banned," and the application logic correctly handles the temporary suspension separately, using `suspended?`, `User.suspended`, and `User.unsuspended` scopes.  It's critical that existing queries, like those for autocomplete and room membership, work as expected *without* modification. It looks like it'll be incredibly clean.

Now, let's drill down into the flooding mechanics, because the existing spec is absolutely crucial.

**Flooding and Cooldown Details:**

*   **Rate Limit:** A bot can send a maximum of 10 messages within any 10-second sliding window. Both API posts *and* webhook replies count towards this limit.
*   **Cooldown Trigger:** When a bot exceeds the limit (e.g., sends the 11th message in a 10-second period), the message is rejected. This rejected message *starts* a 30-second cooldown period, not before.
*   **Cooldown Response:** During the cooldown, the API endpoint responds with a `429 Too Many Requests` HTTP status code, along with a `Retry-After` header. This header gives the client (the bot in our case) the number of seconds remaining in the cooldown (which must be an integer, not a floating point). Webhook replies are *not* posted during the cooldown.
*   **Suspension Trigger:** The crucial point is: *five more attempts* to post during the same cooldown period *suspend the bot*. Not counting the message that started the cooldown!

**Key Questions and Implications:**

1.  **Response to the 11th Message (cooldown starts):** The 11th message (the one that *triggers* the cooldown) *starts* the cooldown but is rejected. It results in a `429` with `Retry-After: 30`.

2.  **Response to the 16th Message (suspension triggered):** The 16th message (the fifth attempt *during* the cooldown, which suspends the bot) MUST return `403 Forbidden`. The key is: this message *suspends* the bot, so a `Retry-After` header would be misleading (the bot is permanently blocked until reactivated).  Any subsequent requests should also get `403`.  Think about how a human and automated tests will test for and expect this.

3.  **`Retry-After` Calculation:**  The `Retry-After` header should represent the *integer* number of seconds remaining in the cooldown. We'll use `.ceil` and make sure it never goes below 1 second.  The cooldown expiration time is fixed when it starts, and `Retry-After` counts down from there.

4.  **Cooldown Reset:**  Importantly, the "attempts during the same cooldown" don't carry over. After a 30-second cooldown expires, the counter is reset.

5.  **Counting messages (across multiple rooms):**  The flooding limit applies to a bot's activity *across all rooms*.  So if a bot posts 6 messages in Room A and 4 messages in Room B within a 10-second window, it's at the limit; the 11th message, in *any* room, will trigger a cooldown.  This is based on timestamps and `created_at`.
    The crucial thing is, to allow reactivations to work correctly, any mechanism for tracking the flood window (either counting the messages or storing timestamps) *must be reset* on reactivation. This means using `created_at` in the database, with a reset to the last reactivated timestamp.

My brain is fully on the problem now. I think I've covered all the edge cases and understood exactly how this will work in code.

          update_data_with_schema_defaults

          new_data.each { |k, v| public_send "#{k}=", v }

            key = method_name.to_s.remove(/(\?|=)/)

And in `BotsController#update`, we have `@bot.touch` whenever the name or avatar is updated, along with `@bot.messages.touch_all`.  If we updated the user on every message, that would invalidate the avatar URL way too often.

Okay, let's look at the data model options:

*   **Option 1**: Should we stick with storing failure counts on `webhooks`? What happens if a bot's webhook fails, we've got `consecutive_failures`, and then someone edits the webhook URL? Ah, DHH and 37signals' design in Rails models is helpful! `User::Bannable` pairs with a `Ban` model; `User::Bot` might pair with a `Webhook` model.

Okay, let's focus on the state a bot needs for misbehavior protection. We need to break this down:

1.  **Suspension State (Persisted)**:  We need a way to indicate if a bot is suspended and the reason.  Options are adding `suspension_reason` (string, nullable) and `suspended_at` (datetime, nullable) columns directly on `users`, a separate `bot_suspensions` (or `suspensions`) table, or even just columns on `users`. *When* a bot is suspended or reactivated, bumping `user.updated_at` is fine. **Webhook Delivery Deep Dive**

Okay, so Ruby 3.4 will have all errors inheriting from `StandardError`, which is great for consistent error handling. I need to make sure I'm rescuing HTTP delivery errors at the right level, looking at `Webhook#deliver` versus `Webhook#post_payload`. The current approach in `deliver` is too broad.

Specifically, the HTTP delivery outcome should be handled *within* `post_payload`. The `post_payload` method is the one sending the HTTP request. If `post_payload` throws an exception, like a timeout or SSL error, I should log a warning, call `record_failed_delivery!`, and return `nil`. If it succeeds, I need to check the HTTP response. If it's a success code, call `record_successful_delivery!`, and *then* proceed to post the reply. If it's *not* a success code (e.g., 500, 404), I need to call `record_failed_delivery!` (incrementing the failure count) and *not* post a reply. If it reaches 10 failures it will suspend the bot.

I also need to remember the `active_recipient_in?(room)` check. If this returns `false` (because the bot is suspended, or removed from the room, etc.), `post_payload` isn't even called, and the failure count isn't touched. Plus, I need to keep in mind the potential for database issues when dealing with Resque and enqueued jobs. If a batch of jobs runs, and a bot gets suspended mid-batch, subsequent jobs shouldn't attempt deliveries. That's good, if that's what is happening.

**Webhook Replies and Flooding**

Okay, now let's carefully go through the "Flooding & Cooldown" section. I have to think about what counts as a "webhook reply" and how it impacts the posting limits.

A `204 No Content` response from a webhook isn't a reply since the bot chooses not to reply synchronously. So, it doesn't count against the limit. However, a `200 OK` with a valid body does count as a webhook reply. If the bot replies synchronously, that will count.

Let's trace:

*   **Normal:** If a synchronous reply is made when there are < 10 messages in 10s, it is posted and counts toward the limit.
*   **11th Message:** If that synchronous reply goes over the limit, it's rejected, and the 30-second cooldown starts.
*   **Cooldown:** During the cooldown, the reply is *rejected*, and the 429 status is returned. However, the question is, *does the webhook still receive the mention or call, and if it synchronously tries to reply, does that count as a failed attempt to post during the cooldown?*
*   **Cooldown Attempts:** If a synchronous webhook reply (a reply body within the 200 OK) is made during the cooldown, *those replies also count* as attempts to post. If the bot tries 5 times during the cooldown (and fails each time), the bot is suspended.

Here's the critical point: the flooding and cooldown mechanisms should be unified for API posts and webhook replies! If I use a single `user.post_bot_message` method on `User::Bot` for API messages and synchronous webhook replies (which is what I should do!), everything will click into place perfectly. Normal posts will work as expected, and during a cooldown, a failed reply increments the cooldown attempt count.

Yes, it does seem to be working exactly as the prompt claims. A suspended bot gets *no* webhooks. During the cooldown, it *does* receive webhooks, but the webhook replies are rejected and the attempt count is incremented. That makes sense.

**Webhook Timeouts and Testing**

Now, I'm checking the Webhook timeouts. The `OPEN_TIMEOUT`, `READ_TIMEOUT`, and `WRITE_TIMEOUT` are set to 10 seconds, 30 seconds, and 10 seconds, respectively.

This brings up a point about QA auto-tests. If the QA tests failing webhooks using dummy servers, the tests are fast, but if the QA uses a server that has timeouts, there may be an issue. If each timeout takes 30 seconds, and if there are 10 failures, that takes a lot longer. I'll need to check if these timeout constants are used in the tests to see if these numbers were explicitly intended.

Now, concerning failing webhooks and bot suspension, we need to trace EVERY possible edge case. It's not just about hitting 10 failures; it's about the sequence, concurrent job handling, and any changes to the webhook URL. The system needs to use atomic SQL/row locking to ensure that the failure count is handled correctly, even when concurrent jobs are running. Additionally, successful deliveries (`2xx` responses) should reset the count immediately, and we can optimize this to avoid writing to the database if the count is already zero. If a bot's webhook URL changes, a successful delivery to the new URL will reset the failure counter. We'll make sure to store webhook failures on the `users` table so we don't accidentally lose any historic data during bot reconfigurations. Reactivation on the admin side is essential. **Deep Dive into Bot Cooldowns and Suspension**

Now, let's really put on the expert hat and dissect this code with a fine-toothed comb, leaving no stone unturned. We need comprehensive model, controller, integration, and even real-browser tests for all these edge cases.

First, the *blank request body during cooldown*! Let's carefully follow the execution path in `User::Bot::Suspendable#deliver_bot_message`:
If the bot is suspended, it returns a `:suspended` status. Otherwise, if cooling down, `record_cooldown_attempt!` kicks in, immediately returning a `429 Too Many Requests` status with `Retry-After` (or a `403` on the 5th attempt). If the bot isn't cooling down, `attempt_message_delivery` checks if the `message.valid?` and a blank body would return a `422`. The critical edge case here: what happens if the 11th message, which *starts* the cooldown, is blank? Because `message.valid?` is checked *before* the cooldown logic, a blank message gets a `422`, while a valid message will correctly hit the limit and begin the cooldown. Perfect! The message that crosses the limit is the one that sets off the 30-second timer.

Next, a bot in cooldown trying to post to a room it's not a member of. `Messages::ByBotsController` comes into play.
`before_action :authenticate_bot` protects against invalid keys (401). `before_action :ensure_unsuspended_bot` protects against suspended bots (403). `before_action :set_room` guards against non-existent rooms or bots not in the room (404). Finally, in the `create` action, `deliver_bot_message` delivers the right cooldown response (429 + `Retry-After`). Clean and standard!

Now, the *crucial* check: the `UsersController#show` view (`app/views/users/show.html.erb`). I need to be sure the suspension doesn't have unintended consequences. The code there:
The view uses the `@user.banned?` for CSS classing, and a blank page for an avatar. There's nothing in lines 24-44 of `app/views/users/show.html.erb` that breaks for a suspended bot! I’m still cautious, though. I should double-check that view more thoroughly at a later time.

Finally, QA auto-tests, which navigate to the bots page to interact with the "Suspended" message, the reason, and the "Reactivate" button. It's time to trace the user journey in the browser!

steps.reasoning_content:
**Automated Testing: Suspension Logic**

Okay, first things first, that `.min-width` fix is elegant! It ensures the text wraps cleanly in that `.flex` container, preventing those buttons from getting pushed off screen. Now, let's get down to brass tacks: testing this suspension logic *thoroughly*. I need to cover every scenario, every edge case, to ensure this feature is robust.

Starting with the model unit tests, I'll focus on the core logic: the flooding rate limit and the cooldown. I'll test the scenarios of up to 10 messages being sent in 10 seconds succeeding, and the messages sent after. I'll need to check the sliding window, which means making sure messages are rejected correctly based on the most recent 10-second window. Both API and webhook replies should factor into the 10-message limit, but not a 204 or non-reply 200 webhooks. Invalid messages before a cooldown shouldn't count, either. The cooldown itself must be tested thoroughly. Messages must be rejected during the cooldown, and *`retry_after`* should reflect the remaining time. I'll need to confirm that attempted posts during the cooldown correctly keep the bot in cooldown until the full 30 seconds elapse. Then, the bot needs to be suspended on the 5th attempt in the same cooldown.

Next up, failing webhooks. Any non-2xx response, timeouts, or connection errors should count as failures. Nine in a row will not suspend the bot, but ten will. I need to make sure a successful 2xx delivery after a streak of failures resets the failure count and prevents immediate suspension. I need to test that a suspended bot behaves correctly: stays in its rooms, still counts toward the owner's bot limit, receives *no* webhooks, and doesn't affect other bots. Finally, reactivation: `reactivate` needs to clear the suspension, reset everything, and allow the bot to post and receive webhooks immediately.

Moving on to controller and integration tests, I'll test the end-to-end flow with flooding via API requests and mixed webhook replies. I'll need to simulate the cooldown, retry-after headers, and the suspension after multiple attempts. I'll check that a webhook during cooldown correctly increments the attempt count. Of course, invalid `bot_key` and deactivated bots should be rejected with the appropriate error codes. I will test failing webhook scenarios: making sure suspended bots receive no further webhooks, even when mentioned or added to a room. Editing a room containing a suspended bot should also retain the bot's room membership.

Finally, I'll need to cover the bots page and reactivation permissions. A suspended bot should stay listed for both its owner and administrators, with the correct suspension reason displayed. Regular members should not see the "Reactivate" button, and their attempts to reactivate should be forbidden. Administrators should see the button, and reactivation should be successful, removing the "Suspended" indicator and enabling immediate posting and webhook receipt. I also need to make sure a suspended bot contributes toward the owner's bot limit and that the owner can still edit or delete it, even while suspended.

Time to write these tests!

steps.reasoning_content:
**Real Browser Testing: A Critical Step**

Okay, so the initial unit tests passed with flying colors – 8 runs, 197 assertions, no failures, no errors. That's a good start, but it's not the whole story. Now, I need to test the *real* browser flow. I'm going to fire up `/usr/bin/chromium --headless --remote-debugging-port=9222` and point it at the live Rails server. This is where the rubber meets the road.

The value here is immense. In a real headless Chromium instance, all that JavaScript – Importmap, Stimulus, `@hotwired/turbo-rails` – actually *executes*. It's not just mocked; it's the real deal. This allows me to test complex interactions, specifically the "Reactivate" flow and the crucial interception of the native `confirm()` dialog. This is handled using the Chrome DevTools Protocol, which is fantastic.

Here's the plan:

*   First, I'll click "Reactivate" and *dismiss* the confirm dialog (accept: false). I need to verify that the dialog type is indeed "confirm", that the bot's state remains "Suspended", and that the "Reactivate" button is still present.
*   Then, I'll repeat the process, but this time I'll *accept* the confirm dialog (accept: true). This should trigger a Turbo DELETE request to `/bots/:bot_id/suspension`. I'll verify the redirect to `/bots` happens correctly, that "Suspended" and "Reactivate" disappear, and that the bot's HTTP endpoint returns a 201 Created status.

Crucially, I also need to verify that a regular member, signed in and capped, sees the expected behavior: "Suspended" and its reason on `/bots`, *no* "Reactivate" button, and the "You've reached the limit..." message when they're at their bot cap.

I'll run a temporary, one-off CDP verification script – no committed files – to get this real-browser, end-to-end behavior validated. This is key to ensuring everything behaves as expected in the production environment.

# Minimal WebSocket client for Chrome DevTools Protocol
class CDPClient
  def initialize(ws_url)
    uri = URI.parse(ws_url)
    @sock = TCPSocket.new(uri.host, uri.port)
    key = Base64.strict_encode64(Random.bytes(16))
    req = "GET #{uri.request_uri} HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: #{uri.host}:#{uri.port}\r\nUpgrade: websocket\r\nConnection: Upgrade\r\nSec-WebSocket-Key: #{key}\r\nSec-WebSocket-Version: 13\r\n\r\n"
    @sock.write(req)
    header = +""
    header << @sock.readpartial(1024) until header.include?("\r\n\r\n")
    raise "WS handshake failed: #{header}" unless header.start_with?("HTTP/1.1 101")
    @id = 0
    @events = []
  end

  def call(method, params = {})
    @id += 1
    target_id = @id
    send_frame(JSON.generate({ id: target_id, method: method, params: params }))
    loop do
      msg = JSON.parse(read_frame)
      if msg["id"] == target_id
        raise "CDP error: #{msg["error"]}" if msg["error"]
        return msg["result"]
      else
        @events << msg
      end
    end
  end

  def drain_events(timeout: 0.3)
    deadline = Time.now + timeout
    while Time.now < deadline
      ready = IO.select([@sock], nil, nil, [deadline - Time.now, 0.01].max)
      break unless ready
      @events << JSON.parse(read_frame)
    end
    @events
  end

  def events
    @events
  end

  def close
    @sock.close rescue nil
  end

  private
    def send_frame(payload)
      bytes = payload.b
      len = bytes.bytesize
      header = [0x81].pack("C")
      if len < 126
        header << [0x80 | len].pack("C")
      elsif len < 65536
        header << [0x80 | 126, len].pack("Cn")
      else
        header << [0x80 | 127, len].pack("CQ>")
      end
      mask = Random.bytes(4)
      masked = bytes.bytes.each_with_index.map { |b, i| b ^ mask.getbyte(i % 4) }.pack("C*")
      @sock.write(header + mask + masked)
    end

    def read_frame
      b1, b2 = @sock.read(2).unpack("CC")
      len = b2 & 0x7f
      if len == 126
        len = @sock.read(2).unpack1("n")
      elsif len == 127
        len = @sock.read(8).unpack1("Q>")
      end
      mask = (b2 & 0x80) != 0 ? @sock.read(4) : nil
      data = @sock.read(len)
      if mask
        data = data.bytes.each_with_index.map { |b, i| b ^ mask.getbyte(i % 4) }.pack("C*")
      end
      data.force_encoding("UTF-8")
    end

  raise "Kevin should see Suspended" unless kevin_page_text.include?("Suspended")

    raise "WS handshake failed: #{header}" unless header.start_with?("HTTP/1.1 101")

    @events = []

    @id += 1
    target_id = @id

**Adding Bot Misbehavior Protection to the Documentation**

Alright, the core issue is clear: we need to document the Bot Misbehavior Protection & Suspension system. Seems like a straightforward task, and the best place for it is likely within the existing `docs/bots.md` file. cat <<'EOF' >> docs/bots.md

## Misbehaving Bot Protection & Suspension (`User::Bot::Suspendable` + `Bots::SuspensionsController`)

- **Fixed Thresholds (Code Constants in `User::Bot::Suspendable`)**:
  - `FLOOD_MESSAGE_LIMIT = 10` within `FLOOD_WINDOW = 10.seconds`.
  - `COOLDOWN_DURATION = 30.seconds`, `COOLDOWN_SUSPENSION_ATTEMPTS = 5`.
  - `WEBHOOK_FAILURE_LIMIT = 10` consecutive failed deliveries.
- **Database-Backed State**: Stored on `users` (`suspended_at`, `suspension_reason`, `bot_cooldown_until`, `bot_cooldown_attempts`, `bot_post_timestamps`, `bot_webhook_failures`) and updated under `with_lock` so web workers (`Messages::ByBotsController`) and background workers (`Webhook::DeliveryJob`) coordinate atomically across processes without touching `updated_at` on routine message deliveries.
- **Flooding & Cooldown**:
  - Both `Messages::ByBotsController#create` and synchronous `Webhook#post_reply` route message posting through `User#deliver_bot_message`.
  - Up to 10 messages in any sliding 10-second window are posted. The 11th message within 10 seconds is rejected and starts a 30-second cooldown (`bot_cooldown_until = now + 30.seconds`, `bot_cooldown_attempts = 0`).
  - During the cooldown, `POST /rooms/:room_id/:bot_key/messages` responds `429 Too Many Requests` with `Retry-After` (remaining seconds), and synchronous webhook replies are suppressed.
  - Five additional attempts during the same cooldown suspend the bot (`reason: "Flooding (too many messages)"`). If the cooldown expires first, `bot_cooldown_attempts` resets on any future cooldown.
- **Failing Webhooks**:
  - `Webhook#deliver_payload` treats any `2xx` (`Net::HTTPSuccess`) as a successful delivery (resetting `bot_webhook_failures` to `0`) and any non-`2xx` status, timeout, or connection/protocol exception as a failed delivery.
  - Ten consecutive failed deliveries suspend the bot (`reason: "Failing webhooks (10 failed deliveries)"`).
- **Suspended Bot Behavior & Reactivation**:
  - Keeping `status: :active` while setting `suspended_at` / `suspension_reason` ensures suspended bots retain all rooms and messages, remain editable/deletable, stay listed on `/bots` as `"Suspended"` with their reason, and continue counting towards `Account#settings.bots_per_member`.
  - Suspended bots receive `403 Forbidden` from `Messages::ByBotsController` and receive no `joined` or `mention` webhooks (`User.unsuspended` scopes in `Room` and `Membership`, plus `Webhook#active_recipient_in?`).
  - Only administrators see the `"Reactivate"` button (with native `confirm()` via `data-turbo-confirm`) on `/bots` and are authorized for `DELETE /bots/:bot_id/suspension` (`Bots::SuspensionsController#destroy`), which calls `User#reactivate` to clear suspension, cooldown, flood window, and webhook failure counters.
EOF

steps.message:
I have implemented automatic bot flood rate-limiting, webhook failure tracking, bot suspension, and administrator reactivation:

- **Flood protection & cooldown (`User::Bot::Suspendable`, `Messages::ByBotsController`, `Webhook`)**:
  - Bots may post at most 10 messages in any sliding 10-second window across both `POST /rooms/:room_id/:bot_key/messages` and synchronous webhook replies.
  - Exceeding 10 messages in 10 seconds rejects the message and starts a 30-second cooldown, returning `429 Too Many Requests` with a `Retry-After` header (seconds remaining) from the posting endpoint and suppressing synchronous webhook replies.
  - Five additional attempts to post during the same cooldown suspend the bot with reason `"Flooding (too many messages)"`.
- **Failing webhooks (`Webhook`, `User::Bot::Suspendable`)**:
  - Any response other than `2xx`, timeout, or connection/network error is counted as a failed webhook delivery; any `2xx` response resets the consecutive failure counter.
  - Ten failed deliveries in a row suspend the bot with reason `"Failing webhooks (10 failed deliveries)"`.
- **Suspended bots & reactivation (`Bots::SuspensionsController`, `app/views/bots/_bot.html.erb`, `Room`, `Membership`, `Webhook`)**:
  - Suspended bots receive `403 Forbidden` from the posting endpoint, receive no webhooks, retain their rooms and messages, continue counting towards their owner's bot limit, and remain listed on `/bots` showing `"Suspended"` with the reason.
  - Only administrators see and can use the `"Reactivate"` button on `/bots`, which uses `data-turbo-confirm` (the browser's native `confirm()` dialog) and resets the bot's suspension, cooldown, flood window, and webhook failure state.

Submitting the final output now.
